| Part | Topic | Time (incl. TRY IT) | Start by |
|------|-------|---------------------|----------|
| 1 | Set up (pre-filled) | 3 min | 0:00 |
| 2 | Writing your first function | 13 min | 0:03 |
| 3 | Functions that use data | 16 min | 0:16 |
| 4 | `if` / `else` | 14 min | 0:32 |
| 5 | `for` loops | 15 min | 0:46 |
| 6 | Iteration the tidyverse way: `map()` and `walk()` | 14 min | 1:01 |
|   | Wrap-up | 5 min | 1:15 |
|   | **Total** | **80 min** | |

**Running behind? Skip in this order:**

1.  TRY IT 6 (map and walk): assign it as homework. Part (b) repeats the district loop from TRY IT 5.
2.  Follow along 6.3 (`walk()`): show it on screen 1 and let learners read it.
3.  The 🧩 "Reading a function call" box in Part 6: point to it on screen 2 and move on.

Don't cut the Part 5 loop (Follow along 5.3 and TRY IT 5): it's the payoff of the session.

**Never speed-run.** If you reach the end of the time, stop at the end of a part and point learners to the rest of the lesson page.

## Before you start

-   This session is **optional / advanced**: it builds on everything before it, especially vectors and subsetting (Session 4) and plotting (Sessions 6–7).
-   Learners need `processed_data/combined_linelist.rds` and `processed_data/measles_final.rds` (saved in Session 3; ready-made copies are in `processed_data/`), and an `outputs/` folder for the saved plots.
-   Learners open `student_scripts/Session 8 - Programming_STUDENT.R`. The filled-in script is `solutions/Session 8 - Programming_SOLUTIONS.R`.
-   Sticky notes as usual: green = done with the TRY IT, red = need help.

## Teaching notes by part

**The motivating example.** Keep returning to it: *"Your manager wants an epidemic curve for every hospital, every week."* By the end, one loop does it.

**Part 1 — Set up.** The `library()` and `import()` lines are already in the student script: learners just run them. Only the measles import (TRY IT 1) is typed.

**Part 2 — Writing your first function.** Show that a function only exists after you run the whole block — it then appears in the **Variables** pane. When you change a function, re-run the block, or R keeps using the old version. Point out that `c_to_f()` is vectorized because the maths inside is, so it works inside `mutate()`. The `f_to_c(104.7)` result (40.4) is the Fahrenheit temperature learners found in the measles data in Session 1.

**Part 3 — Functions that use data.** Point out that `pct()` replaces the `round(mean(...) * 100, 1)` learners wrote over and over in Session 5, and that `paste("Weekly cases:", hospital)` gives every plot the right title. In TRY IT 3, watch for learners naming the argument `district`: then `filter(district == district)` compares the column with itself and keeps every row — no error, just the wrong answer (n = 1163 instead of 342). That's why the argument is called `district_name`. The lesson page has this as a warning box.

After Follow along 3.2, open the 🤔 "it ran without an error, but is it right?" box: `hospital_summary(linelist, "Military hospital")` (lower-case "h") gives 0 cases and `NaN`, with no error. Ask the class what would happen if this ran inside a report every week. Part 4 comes back to it with `stopifnot()`.

**Part 4 — `if` / `else`.** Run `fever_status(c(39.2, 36.9))` live so learners see the error "the condition has length > 1": `if` asks one yes/no question. Then switch to the vectorized `if_else()` from Session 2. Present `stop()` input checks as where `if` really shines. (Both error chunks are deliberate; the lesson page shows the errors.) `stopifnot()` is reading only: show on screen 2 how one line fixes the silent typo from Part 3, so `"Military hospital"` now stops with an error instead of returning 0.

**Part 5 — `for` loops.** The smallest loop (two hospital names) is reading only: read it aloud from the screen ("for each `h` in this vector..."), then have learners type Follow along 5.1. Stress that inside a loop nothing prints automatically (`print()`), and that results need a container created **before** the loop. In the payoff loop, point out `make_clean_names()` turning "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital" into `st_marks_maternity_hospital` and `paste0()` building the file name: six files, one loop — and next week you just re-run it. Have learners check the **Explorer** for the new files in `outputs/`. Remind them that `mutate()`, `group_by()` + `summarise()`, and `across()` already loop for them; a `for` loop is for repeating a **whole task**.

**Part 6 — `map()` and `walk()`.** Point out that a data frame is a list of columns, so `map_dbl()` runs once per column, and that `~ .x` is the same shorthand they used with `across()` in Session 3. Loop or `map()`? Both are fine — tell learners to use the one they can read.

**🔁 `lapply()` / `sapply()` (reading only, 2 min).** Learners who go on to bioinformatics will meet these constantly: Bioconductor code and vignettes use the apply family far more than purrr. Show the translation table on screen 2, then let the class predict what `sapply(three_cols, range, na.rm = TRUE)` returns before you scroll to the output: the matrix is the teaching moment for why `map_dbl()` exists. Nobody types it.

**Wrap-up.** Today: `function()`, arguments and defaults, `if`/`else`, `stop()`, `stopifnot()`, `if_else()`, `for` loops, `map()`, `map_dbl()`, `walk()`. The big idea: write it once, run it many times — a function plus a loop (or `walk()`) turns an hour of copy-paste into one line you can re-run every week. Where to go next: [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) (functions and iteration chapters) and [The Epidemiologist R Handbook](https://epirhandbook.com/).
